## Observations

1. Each XOR constraint is an undirected edge labeled \(Z_i\): knowing the value at either endpoint determines the value at the other.
2. In each connected component, fixing the root to zero lets a traversal assign relative values \(P_v\). An edge that disagrees with these values makes the system impossible, because changing the root value XORs the same number into both endpoints and leaves their XOR unchanged.
3. If all edges agree with the relative values, the solutions in a component are exactly \(A_v=P_v\oplus T\), where \(T\) is any non-negative integer. Different components can choose their offsets independently.
4. Each bit contributes independently to the sum. Setting a bit of \(T\) to one flips that bit at every vertex in the component, so it is beneficial exactly when more than half of the relative values have a one there. Only bits 0 through 29 can occur in the relative values.
5. A graph traversal examines each vertex and edge a constant number of times, and optimizing a component requires only 30 bit checks per vertex.

## Solution sketch

> 1. Each XOR constraint is an undirected edge labeled \(Z_i\): knowing the value at either endpoint determines the value at the other.

1. Build an adjacency list, adding each labeled edge in both directions. Keep self-loops and parallel edges so that every input constraint is checked.

> 2. In each connected component, fixing the root to zero lets a traversal assign relative values \(P_v\). An edge that disagrees with these values makes the system impossible, because changing the root value XORs the same number into both endpoints and leaves their XOR unchanged.

2. For each unvisited vertex, start an iterative DFS or BFS with its relative value set to zero. Along an edge from \(u\) to \(v\) labeled \(z\), the required relative value of \(v\) is \(P_u\oplus z\). Assign it if \(v\) is unvisited; otherwise, check that it matches. On any mismatch, print \(-1\) and stop. In particular, this rejects nonzero self-loops and conflicting parallel edges. Collect the vertices of each component as you visit them.

> 4. Each bit contributes independently to the sum. Setting a bit of \(T\) to one flips that bit at every vertex in the component, so it is beneficial exactly when more than half of the relative values have a one there. Only bits 0 through 29 can occur in the relative values.

3. For a component of size \(s\), count the relative values with a one at each bit from 0 through 29. If the count at a bit is \(c\), leaving the offset bit zero gives \(c\) ones, while setting it gives \(s-c\). Set the offset bit only if \(2c>s\); either choice is optimal in a tie. Leave higher bits zero, since setting one would only increase the sum.

> 3. If all edges agree with the relative values, the solutions in a component are exactly \(A_v=P_v\oplus T\), where \(T\) is any non-negative integer. Different components can choose their offsets independently.

4. Apply each component’s chosen offset to its relative values. This preserves every edge XOR and minimizes the sum in that component, hence also the total sum. An isolated vertex gets zero, so when \(M=0\) the answer is all zeros. If no mismatch occurred, print the resulting values in vertex order.

> 5. A graph traversal examines each vertex and edge a constant number of times, and optimizing a component requires only 30 bit checks per vertex.

5. The total time is \(O(N+M+30N)=O(N+M)\) under the given bounds. The adjacency lists, traversal state, component vertices, and answer use \(O(N+M)\) space.
